text:
Qatar deposits instrument of accession to the 1997 Protocol adding Annex VI to MARPOL

Ambassador Sheikh Abdullah bin Mohammed bin Saud Al-Thani met IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez

Annex VI covers sulphur and NOx limits, energy efficiency rules, and would carry the Net-Zero Framework

Qatar has acceded to Annex VI of the MARPOL convention, the part of the treaty that sets sulphur and NOx limits for marine fuels and engines and would carry the IMO's Net-Zero Framework if it is adopted.

The country's ambassador to the UK and permanent representative to the IMO, Sheikh Abdullah bin Mohammed bin Saud Al-Thani, deposited the instrument of accession to the 1997 Protocol at a meeting with IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez at the organisation's London headquarters on Friday, the Qatar News Agency reported.

The two discussed the accession's role in supporting international efforts to reduce air pollution from ships and protect the marine environment, as well as wider cooperation between Qatar and the IMO, according to the agency.

They also discussed developments in the Strait of Hormuz and "the importance of ensuring the safety and continuity of maritime navigation and international trade through vital waterways in accordance with the provisions of international law," it said.

Annex VI entered into force in May 2005, and under the convention's terms a state's accession takes effect three months after the instrument is deposited.

Ships flagged in states that are not party to the annex are already subject to its requirements when calling at the ports of states that are, so the practical effect of accession is to bring Qatar's own flag administration and ports formally within the regime.

title: Climate Group's NTU Study Calls for "Fingerprinting" of Green Bunkers to Stop Feedstock Fraud
description:
ISCC may dominate the market, the authors find, with more than 90% of biofuels in the UK ISCC-certified and 7,546 ISCC certificates issued in 2024 against 72 for RSB.
It also calls for a central database logging every transaction so that the same batch of fuel cannot be claimed as green more than once, pointing to the EU's Union Database as the model.
That is one side of a live debate at the IMO, where the US has proposed regional ILUC risk rules in submission ISWG-GHG 21/3/21.
For Singapore, the report recommends expanding the pool of trained sustainability auditors as well as adopting fingerprinting, which the campaign group says would strengthen the country's position as a trusted green maritime hub.
The framework the certification rules are meant to serve has yet to be adopted: the Net-Zero Framework failed to pass at last October's extraordinary session and is due back before the Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) on November 30, with a resumed adoption session pencilled in for December 4.
text:
Study commissioned by campaign group Pacific Environment, carried out by NTU Singapore's MESD centre

Reviews ISCC, RSB, RenovaBio, California's LCFS, and the US RFS as models for the IMO's certification rules

Recommends chemical testing of fuels and a central database against double-counting

Urges IMO to cap or phase out high-ILUC crop feedstocks; report says MPA reviewed it

The most recent cases of feedstock fraud in biofuel certification involved virgin crop oils being passed off as waste used cooking oil (UCO) and palm oil mill effluent (POME), and were only uncovered when the volumes declared became implausible, according to a study published on Tuesday that argues paper-based checks will not be enough as the IMO writes its own fuel certification rules.

The study was commissioned by Pacific Environment, a US-based climate campaign group, and carried out by the Maritime Energy and Sustainable Development (MESD) centre of excellence at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore, with the port authority MPA reviewing the report before publication, according to its acknowledgements.

It reviews the voluntary ISCC and RSB schemes used under the EU's Renewable Energy Directive and CORSIA, alongside Brazil's RenovaBio, California's Low Carbon Fuel Standard, and the US Renewable Fuel Standard, as blueprints for the sustainable fuel certification schemes (SFCS) the IMO is developing for its Net-Zero Framework.

ISCC may dominate the market, the authors find, with more than 90% of biofuels in the UK ISCC-certified and 7,546 ISCC certificates issued in 2024 against 72 for RSB.

Fingerprinting

To counter feedstock fraud the study recommends chemical testing, or "fingerprinting", to verify what a fuel was made from independently of its paperwork, though it says this is "subject to further methodology development and a cost-benefit analysis", and notes Singapore has already developed such a method using methanol as a case study.

It also calls for a central database logging every transaction so that the same batch of fuel cannot be claimed as green more than once, pointing to the EU's Union Database as the model.

"As shipping scales up the use of these fuels, we need certification systems that are robust enough to guard against fraud and unsustainable production, while also being practical and workable across complex international supply chains," said Pacific Environment's Singapore climate specialist Lim Jie Ying in an emailed press release.

Land Use

The study finds the biggest gap between the schemes is the treatment of indirect land-use change (ILUC), the emissions caused when fuel crops displace food production and drive deforestation elsewhere, which CORSIA and the two US schemes count but the EU schemes do not.

The study's authors recommend a hybrid approach, using quantitative ILUC values to penalise the carbon intensity of crop-based biofuels while still allowing their use, with usage caps or an eventual phase-out for high-risk feedstocks.

That is one side of a live debate at the IMO, where the US has proposed regional ILUC risk rules in submission ISWG-GHG 21/3/21.

"Strengthening the traceability of sustainable fuels through continued research and innovation will be critical in supporting the maritime energy transition," said the study's lead researcher, Dr Yeoh Keat Ping, research lead at MESD.

For Singapore, the report recommends expanding the pool of trained sustainability auditors as well as adopting fingerprinting, which the campaign group says would strengthen the country's position as a trusted green maritime hub.

The framework the certification rules are meant to serve has yet to be adopted: the Net-Zero Framework failed to pass at last October's extraordinary session and is due back before the Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) on November 30, with a resumed adoption session pencilled in for December 4.

text:
IBIA's representative to the IMO, Dr Edmund Hughes. Image Credit: IBIA

Multiplier "could potentially replace financial rewards and so the need for revenues to provide them", says IBIA's Dr Edmund Hughes

Without a fund, cash rewards for zero and near-zero fuels "would not be possible", but a non-fiscal route may work

Several states reviewing positions and may be moderating "red lines" after ISWG-GHG 22

Hughes moderates the regulatory panel at the IBIA Annual Convention in New York, November 10-12

IBIA's representative to the IMO, Dr Edmund Hughes, says China's multiplier proposal for zero and near-zero fuels and technologies could be a way round the deadlock over an IMO fund under the Net-Zero Framework (NZF), rewarding green fuels without needing revenues to pay for it.

"Such a multiplier, if designed correctly, could potentially replace financial rewards and so the need for revenues to provide them," he told Ship & Bunker following last week's ISWG-GHG 22.

The fund has proven a key sticking point for the proposed framework, with the US in particular one of its most outspoken critics, criticism that many feel ultimately led to adoption of the NZF being derailed at an extraordinary session last October.

The US delegation reiterated at ISWG-GHG 22 that an IMO-administered fund remains a red line.

China's proposal would apply the multiplier "where funding for monetary rewards is constrained" and have it "operate effectively in conjunction with the use of Surplus Units."

Hughes said it had received support from several member states at the meeting, but was clear about what losing the fund would mean for cash rewards.

"Without provisions for raising and a depositary for receiving revenues from a global measure it would mean financial rewards for the use of ZNZs would not be possible," he said.

"However, alternative approaches for incentivising uptake of ZNZs through widening the scope and use of Surplus Units and the application of a 'multiplier' might provide a non-fiscal solution if linked to other schemes such as Japan's proposal for 'direct voluntary contributions'."

Japan's contributions concept could also be integrated with other schemes to provide funds for the just and equitable transition that is a core principle of the 2023 IMO GHG strategy, he added.

That is a shift in emphasis from the position IBIA and ICS took in their joint submission calling for significant rewards paid from the framework's fund.

Hughes said industry bodies, ICS and IBIA among them, had backed adoption of the framework primarily to secure global regulation of shipping's GHG emissions and "to reduce the risk of proliferation of national/regional measures such as seen under the European Union".

Red Lines

On the week itself, he said "limited progress" had been made, as it was the first time member states had met to consider the proposals to amend the draft framework circulated since Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) 84 in May, from Brazil, Liberia, Tuvalu, and Japan, and one submitted jointly by Australia, Canada, South Africa, and the UK.

"Despite the remaining divergent views it is evident that following consideration several Member States are reviewing their position and may be moderating their 'red lines' on several of the key policy issues," he said.

A gentler Global Fuel Intensity (GFI) reduction trajectory and greater flexibility in the supply and use of surplus units had been identified by many member states, he said, but they remained divided on the payment by ships for remedial units when unable to comply, and on the establishment of an IMO GHG fund.

Some new proposals had received support, including the idea of a "facility" for managing and disbursing revenues through established institutions rather than the IMO, notably from the US.

"As the Chair of the meeting observed the Group's general view was that the name of the mechanism matters less than its 'nature, purpose and functions' which all remain open for further definition and including how would IMO retain oversight," he said.

The working group closed on Friday with its chair reporting a willingness to present text to MEPC in November, and a UCL readout counting 38 states speaking for a central fund and 17 against.

The topic will be discussed further at the IBIA Annual Convention in New York on November 10-12, where Hughes, who headed the IMO's air pollution and energy efficiency work from 2013 to 2020 and has represented the bunker industry body at the organisation since 2023, moderates the regulatory and policy panel, Navigating a Changing Framework.

text:
Dutch biofuel company Sunoil Biodiesel has received regulatory clearance to supply its sustainable fuel products in Belgium, opening another European market for the company, biofuels international reported.

With the approval, Belgium has joined the growing number of European countries where Sunoil can sell its biodiesel made from waste materials.

The company said expansion into a new country requires systems that can track products properly, meet sustainability standards and comply with local rules at every stage of the supply chain. Sunoil said these measures provide a strong base for its continued expansion across Europe.

The approval comes as the company increases its operations and expands the use of its biodiesel in transport. Sunoil’s inland barge Birjo II has recently been converted to operate completely on B100 biodiesel. The fuel is produced in the Netherlands and supplied through a partnership with BFT Tanker Logistics.

Birjo II is now transporting biofuel using 100% renewable fuel, providing an example of how Sunoil’s biodiesel can be used in transport to reduce emissions.

Sunoil produces biodiesel from certified waste oils and fats at its facilities in Emmen and Kampen. The company also operates a trading business in Amsterdam.

Its biodiesel is used as an alternative to fossil-based diesel or mixed with fossil diesel for use in road transport, shipping and the energy sector.

text:
Environmental non-profit Pacific Environment and Nanyang Technological University, Singapore (NTU Singapore) have issued a new study highlighting that strict and reliable fuel certification is essential to keep the global shipping industry's transition to clean fuels honest and fraud-free.

The study titled “The role of sustainable fuels certification schemes in maritime decarbonisation," was led by the Maritime Energy & Sustainable Development Centre of Excellence (MESD) at NTU Singapore.

It evaluates established certification systems — including those by the International Sustainability & Carbon Certification (ISCC) and Roundtable on Sustainable Biomaterials (RSB), Brazil’s RenovaBio, the California Air Resources Board’s Low Carbon Fuel Standard (CARB LCFS), and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s Renewable Fuel Standard (U.S. EPA RFS) — to guide the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) as it establishes global standards for Sustainable Fuel Certification Schemes (SFCS).

These existing frameworks provide critical blueprints for measuring full-lifecycle carbon emissions, tracking fuel ownership, and ensuring broader environmental sustainability.

Singapore climate specialist Lim Jie Ying, Pacific Environment, said, “Certification systems will play an essential role in ensuring that zero- and near-zero-emission fuels deliver genuine environmental benefits. As shipping scales up the use of these fuels, we need certification systems that are robust enough to guard against fraud and unsustainable production, while also being practical and workable across complex international supply chains.”

The study outlines major gaps in global fuel supply chains that leave them vulnerable to cheating. For example, documented cases of fraud involving recycled waste, such as used cooking oil and palm oil mill effluent, demonstrate the limitations of verification systems relying purely on paper documentation without physical origin checks.

To tackle these risks, the study recommends chemical testing or fuel “fingerprinting” to verify fuel authenticity independently, alongside stronger cross-checks. It also calls for a centralised digital database to log all fuel transactions, preventing suppliers from falsely claiming the same batch of green fuel more than once.

Lead researcher of the study, Dr Yeoh Keat Ping, Research Lead at MESD, NTU Singapore, said: “Strengthening the traceability of sustainable fuels through continued research and innovation will be critical in supporting the maritime energy transition. This requires a combined effort across policy formulation, laboratory validation, digital tools and shared industry knowledge. As traded volumes of sustainable fuels grow, these solutions must be robust enough to keep pace with an evolving landscape.”

Additionally, the study addresses the risk of Indirect Land-Use Change (ILUC), where clearing land for fuel crops causes deforestation and displaces food production elsewhere. It urges the IMO to adopt a balanced risk-based approach to cap or phase out high-risk crop feedstocks, protecting both ecosystems and global food security.

For Singapore, Pacific Environment notes that the study highlights a key opportunity to strengthen the country’s role as a trusted green maritime hub. By expanding training for local sustainability auditors and adopting fuel fingerprinting techniques, Singapore could ensure high supply chain integrity for alternative fuels moving through Southeast Asia.

title: As the IMO continues to stall the UK must take action on maritime emissions
description:
Negotiations at the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) last week have drawn a blank for the third meeting in a row, as US and Saudi-led efforts to derail progress were successful.
The next major IMO meeting takes place from November 30th to December 3rd.
Given the challenges, the UK, itself a champion of an ambitious deal at the IMO, should already be putting contingency plans in place in case a credible deal cannot be reached.
The UK must not let the ongoing delays at the IMO put the brakes on shipping’s need to decarbonise.
Taking action at the national level on international shipping is becoming increasingly urgent in light of the IMO’s failure to move forward for almost a year.
text:
Negotiations at the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) last week have drawn a blank for the third meeting in a row, as US and Saudi-led efforts to derail progress were successful.

The continued failure to find an ambitious agreement on cutting international emissions not only puts shipping off course to decarbonise, but locks fossil fuel importing states and the shipping industry into continued dependency. During the Hormuz crisis, dependence on oil cost the industry roughly £295 million a day, according to T&E estimates.

The next major IMO meeting takes place from November 30th to December 3rd. The UK should push to adopt an ambitious global deal, however, governments will face significant opposition. Putting the adoption of a global deal capable of decarbonising shipping by 2050 at risk.

Given the challenges, the UK, itself a champion of an ambitious deal at the IMO, should already be putting contingency plans in place in case a credible deal cannot be reached. The UK must not let the ongoing delays at the IMO put the brakes on shipping’s need to decarbonise. Taking action at the national level on international shipping is becoming increasingly urgent in light of the IMO’s failure to move forward for almost a year.

The UK Government needs to release its consultation paper on fuel regulation for the maritime sector, for domestic and international voyages, as indicated in the Maritime Decarbonisation Strategy by November 2026. The sector needs certainty on the direction of Government policy, and outlining the planned approach through consultation is the first step in introducing fuel regulation.

description:
The new coalition will focus on one of the biggest challenges facing maritime decarbonisation: ensuring the UK has the fuels, infrastructure and policy framework needed to support shipping’s transition to net zero.
The objectives of the coalition include: – Coordinate industry action to support the shipping sector’s energy transition.
– Provide evidence-based input into the UK Government’s forthcoming consultation on domestic maritime fuel regulation.
– Call for UK ETS maritime revenues to be directed towards maritime decarbonisation, including fuel production, port infrastructure and deployment.
Rhett Hatcher, Chief Executive of the UK Chamber of Shipping, said:“Access to alternative fuels is one of the defining challenges for the future of UK shipping.
text:
The new coalition will focus on one of the biggest challenges facing maritime decarbonisation: ensuring the UK has the fuels, infrastructure and policy framework needed to support shipping’s transition to net zero.

The coalition will be jointly facilitated by the UK Chamber of Shipping and CLIA.

Members include Anaerobic Digestion & Bioresources Association, Carbon Capture and Storage Association (CCSA), eFuel Alliance, Hydrogen UK, IBIA – International Bunkering Industry Association, MI — The Global Methanol Alliance, Renewable Transport Fuel Association, SEA-LNG, and the UK Ammonia Alliance.

The objectives of the coalition include:

– Coordinate industry action to support the shipping sector’s energy transition.

– Provide evidence-based input into the UK Government’s forthcoming consultation on domestic maritime fuel regulation.

– Champion a technology-neutral approach that supports investment in alternative fuels, port infrastructure and enabling technologies.

– Call for UK ETS maritime revenues to be directed towards maritime decarbonisation, including fuel production, port infrastructure and deployment.

Rhett Hatcher, Chief Executive of the UK Chamber of Shipping, said:“Access to alternative fuels is one of the defining challenges for the future of UK shipping. This coalition brings together the companies and organisations needed to turn ambition into delivery.If the UK wants to lead on maritime decarbonisation, industry and government must work together to create the right conditions for investment in fuels, infrastructure and new technologies.”

Andy Harmer, Executive Director, CLIA in the UK & Ireland said:“Shipping’s transition to lower-emissions fuels depends on those fuels being available at scale, in the places ships need them, supported by the necessary infrastructure and a policy framework that encourages investment and innovation.This Coalition brings the maritime, fuel and technology sectors together to help identify practical solutions and support a technology- and fuel-neutral approach based on lifecycle emissions performance.”

The coalition will meet regularly, with the UK Chamber of Shipping and CLIA acting as joint facilitators.

text:
30 countries open to softer near-term GFI targets

Two-tiered GFI structure draws broad support

38 countries back retaining a central financial mechanism

IMAGE: IMO headquarters in London. X of @IMOHQ

The 22nd Intersessional Working Group on Reduction of Greenhouse Gas Emissions from Ships (ISWG-GHG 22) met on 1-4 September to consider proposals addressing concerns over the draft MARPOL Annex VI amendments approved at MEPC 83 in April 2025.

24 member states attending the closed-door meetings favoured retaining the GHG fuel intensity (GFI) reduction targets as approved in April 2025, according to a report by University College London's (UCL) Shipping and Oceans Research Group.

The current version of the Net-Zero Framework (NZF), approved at MEPC 83 in April 2025, introduces a two-tiered greenhouse gas (GHG) fuel standard that would require ships to progressively reduce their well-to-wake GFI from 2028 onwards.

The draft sets the base reduction factor at 65% by 2040.

30 member states were open to easing GFI reduction requirements between 2029-35, the report said.

This included 23 member states that favoured compensating for the softer start with steeper reductions later in the 2030s. But a lack of clarity over the exact targets left the trajectory open to further negotiation, the authors noted.

10 countries backed an approach linking GFI targets more closely to fuel affordability, availability and scalability, as proposed by Liberia and supported by the US.

Discussions also revisited whether the 2040 target approved in April 2025 should remain in the framework. 35 member states backed retaining it, while 16 preferred to remove it and determine the target later.

The two-tier structure of base and direct targets, supported in separate proposals from Brazil, Tuvalu and Japan, drew backing from 30 member states, compared with 17 that favoured Liberia’s proposed single-tier system based only on the base target.

The financial mechanism produced a more pronounced majority.

UCL counted 38 member states supporting a fund, facility or similar structure, while 17 others favoured a technical-only system without a central financial mechanism.

The existing NZF would require non-compliant ships to buy remedial units (RUs), with the revenues flowing into an IMO Net-Zero Fund to support uptake of low- and zero-emission fuels and accelerate a just and equitable transition.

Japan proposed allowing shipowners to instead make equivalent payments directly to eligible projects.

UCL said this proposal was "robustly rejected", highlighting that only 12 countries supported direct contributions, while another 12 explicitly opposed the Japanese concept and 32 backed RU payments.

On the other hand, the Chinese proposal to balance RU and reward payments that could be netted to form a single transaction received broad support, it said. However, several delegations raised concerns over how the system would work in practice, with the details still to be developed through guidelines.

32 countries favoured retaining a specific incentive for the use of low- and zero-emission fuels, while 14 argued that a separate reward was not needed or opposed it.

29 delegations were open to further consideration of a multiplier that could award additional surplus units to promote the use of low- and zero-emission fuels, while nine opposed it. Its interaction with the existing ZNZ reward mechanism remains unresolved.

There was "clear potential for a return to a strong policy solution" this year, but uncertainty remained over support for the industry's transition and lower-income countries, lead report author Tristan Smith said.

While member states did not reach a consensus, ISWG-GHG chair Sveinung Oftedal said delegations had shown a "genuine willingness" to make further progress. The group invited delegations to work between sessions towards proposals that could attract greater convergence.

Discussions will continue at ISWG-GHG 23 on 23-27 November, ahead of MEPC 85 on 30 November to 3 December. ISWG-GHG 23 will also include discussions on the IMO’s lifecycle GHG assessment (LCA) framework, which were deferred because of time constraints.

Any revised text emerging from MEPC 85 could then be put forward for adoption at the second extraordinary session, scheduled to resume on 4 December, subject to discussions at MEPC 85.

By Konica Bhatt

Japanese trading firm Itochu has bought into India’s “first independent” ammonia storage terminal ahead of a separate green ammonia offtake deal in the country.
The firm acquired an undisclosed portion of Aegis Vopak Terminals’ Port Pipavav project, which features a 36,000-tonne ammonia storage tank.

Ammonia continues to gain prominence as a clean maritime fuel as ship operators seek decarbonisation in line with international authorities.
While criticised for challenges around combustion efficiency and toxicity, green ammonia offers compatibility with existing global infrastructures as well as emerging marine technologies.

The firm acquired an undisclosed portion of Aegis Vopak Terminals’ Port Pipavav project, which features a 36,000-tonne ammonia storage tank.

The facility at the “strategic port” in western India features ammonia handling infrastructure such as pipelines and loading facilities and was completed for operation in August.

The transaction of undisclosed value follows the trader securing 300,000 tonnes of green ammonia per year from Larsen & Toubro Greentech, which will supply the full capacity of its Kandla, India, plant to fulfil the agreement.

The port could provide access to shipping in the Arabian Sea towards the Middle East and eastern Africa, alongside routes toward Southeast Asia and Australia via the Bay of Bengal and Indian Ocean.

Itochu’s specialised bunkering vessel, due to be built in Singapore, is expected to be used in the firm’s maritime operations upon its scheduled September 2027 delivery.

Ammonia continues to gain prominence as a clean maritime fuel as ship operators seek decarbonisation in line with international authorities.

While criticised for challenges around combustion efficiency and toxicity, green ammonia offers compatibility with existing global infrastructures as well as emerging marine technologies.

text:
Eighteen of the world’s leading maritime nations have issued an unusually stark warning that the international rules underpinning global shipping are being eroded, threatening to fragment both maritime markets and global trade.

The CSG argued that maritime transport should now be viewed as critical infrastructure underpinning not only trade but global food and energy security.

The warning goes well beyond the current battle over the Strait of Hormuz. The CSG pointed to covid, the war in Ukraine, drought at the Panama Canal and conflict in the Middle East as repeated demonstrations of how vulnerable maritime supply chains have become. It also highlighted discriminatory trade measures and the proliferation of different national and regional approaches to shipping regulation.

Uncertainty over whether ships will retain access to particular ports or routes directly affects long-term commercial planning, the group argued, while fragmented regulation ultimately fragments markets and raises costs.

Shipping routes, once largely treated as neutral conduits for trade, are increasingly being used as geopolitical leverage. Hormuz provides the most immediate example. Iran has sought to impose greater control over merchant traffic through the strait while attacks on commercial shipping have multiplied, challenging the assumption that international chokepoints will remain reliably open to neutral trade.

The CSG is an international forum of major maritime nations dedicated to promoting open, fair, and competitive global maritime transport. It brings together countries from Europe, Asia, and North America to consult on key shipping policies and regulatory challenges.

The CSG stressed that the answer is not simply to write more regulations, but to apply existing international rules more consistently.

It singled out the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, including rights of innocent and transit passage, while describing the International Maritime Organization as the central global forum for maintaining navigation, safety, security and fair competition.

The group also took aim at the explosive growth of the shadow fleet created by sanctions on Russia and Iran.

Hundreds of ships now operate outside conventional insurance, safety and transparency frameworks, the CSG said, creating parallel maritime systems that bypass environmental and safety standards.

“The result is a two-tier system, one governed by rules, the other by opacity,” the statement warned.

Industry estimates put the wider shadow tanker fleet at more than 1,500 vessels, approaching a fifth of global tanker capacity.

The CSG’s prescription is greater cooperation between maritime nations, consistent enforcement across jurisdictions, better information exchange and renewed political backing for multilateral institutions.

The statement culminates in a direct appeal for maritime states to defend freedom of navigation and prevent fragmentation becoming embedded within shipping networks.

“When shipping supply chains fragment, the global economy fragments with it,” the CSG warned.

Many of the same concerns will form the backdrop to the opening Big Issues session at Splash Singapore, Asia’s leading shipping conference, at the Fairmont Hotel on September 24.

The session will examine the forces reshaping shipping beyond the normal market-cycle debate, with particular emphasis on how organisations should operate when geopolitics, regulation, technology and commercial risk collide.

The discussion will ask how companies should structure themselves, allocate risk, maintain fast decision-making, retain talent and avoid paralysis when visibility is poor and long-established assumptions can no longer be relied upon.

On stage will be Bjorn Hojgaard of shipmanagement giant Anglo-Eastern, Hor Weng Yew of Pacific Carriers, Swire Shipping CEO Jeremy Sutton, John Su of Erasmus Shipinvest, AET president Nick Potter and X-Press Feeders CEO Shmuel Yoskovitz.

title: The Future of Green Shipping: How Alternative Fuels Are Cleaning Up Our Oceans | Earth
description:

The Primary Contenders Replacing Heavy Fuel Oil Because commercial vessels vary widely in size, cargo weight, and voyage distance, ship operators are testing and deploying several distinct alternative fuels.
Compared to standard heavy fuel oil, LNG reduces sulfur oxide emissions by nearly 99% and cuts nitrogen oxide emissions by up to 85%.
When blended or swapped with biomethane (Bio-LNG) derived from organic waste, overall lifecycle carbon emissions decrease significantly without requiring major modifications to existing gas engines.

text:
Beyond Heavy Fuel Oil: The Primary Alternatives

When discussing global carbon reduction efforts, public attention usually centers on electric passenger cars, solar installations, and onshore wind farms. Yet floating across the open ocean is an industry responsible for carrying more than 80% of all globally traded goods: commercial shipping.

Massive container ships, bulk carriers, and chemical tankers form the invisible backbone of international commerce. However, these vessels traditionally rely on heavy fuel oil, a dense residue of the crude oil refining process that produces high levels of greenhouse gases, sulfur oxides, and particulate matter. As international environmental standards become more strict—led by targets established by the International Maritime Organization (IMO)—the maritime sector faces a structural shift toward cleaner power sources.

Transitioning a global fleet away from petroleum requires introducing a combination of alternative energy solutions rather than relying on a single replacement.

The Primary Contenders Replacing Heavy Fuel Oil

Because commercial vessels vary widely in size, cargo weight, and voyage distance, ship operators are testing and deploying several distinct alternative fuels. Each option presents unique advantages and operational trade-offs.

1. Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) and Bio-LNG

Liquefied Natural Gas represents one of the most widely adopted alternative fuels currently in service. Compared to standard heavy fuel oil, LNG reduces sulfur oxide emissions by nearly 99% and cuts nitrogen oxide emissions by up to 85%.

While fossil-derived LNG still produces carbon dioxide during combustion, it serves as a stepping stone toward cleaner variants. When blended or swapped with biomethane (Bio-LNG) derived from organic waste, overall lifecycle carbon emissions decrease significantly without requiring major modifications to existing gas engines.

2. Green Methanol

Methanol is rapidly gaining favor among major international container shipping lines. One of its primary benefits is physical handling: unlike cryogenic gases, liquid methanol remains stable at normal atmospheric temperatures and pressures, simplifying onboard storage and bunkering infrastructure.

When produced using captured carbon dioxide and renewable energy (e-methanol) or agricultural biomass (bio-methanol), green methanol provides a near-zero carbon lifecycle. As a result, shipbuilders are seeing a steady rise in dual-fuel engine orders capable of running on both traditional marine fuels and methanol.

3. Green Ammonia and Hydrogen

For long-distance, deep-sea voyages, hydrogen and ammonia represent key zero-carbon possibilities. Ammonia contains no carbon molecules, meaning its combustion generates no direct carbon dioxide emissions.

However, widespread deployment of ammonia faces practical hurdles. Ammonia is toxic to human exposure and requires specialized safety protocols, secondary containment systems, and rigorous crew training. Furthermore, producing green ammonia at scale requires massive amounts of renewable electricity to generate clean hydrogen feedstock. Despite these challenges, ammonia remains a prominent long-term option for long-haul ocean transport.

4. Wind-Assisted Propulsion and Hybrid Systems

Alongside liquid and gaseous fuels, mechanical wind technologies are returning to modern cargo ships. Advanced rotor sails, rigid wings, and computer-controlled kites utilize ocean winds to assist main engine propulsion.

When paired with onboard battery energy storage and hybrid electric systems, wind-assist technologies can lower fuel consumption by 10% to 20% on optimal trade routes, reducing both operational costs and total exhaust emissions.

Regulatory Drivers and Operational Challenges

The acceleration toward green shipping is driven largely by strict regulatory frameworks. Frameworks like the IMO’s Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) rate ships on their operational efficiency, encouraging vessel owners to reduce emissions or risk operational penalties. Concurrently, regional policies such as the European Union’s FuelEU Maritime initiative mandate a progressive reduction in the greenhouse gas intensity of energy used on board ships.

However, moving from trial projects to full fleet adoption requires overcoming significant infrastructure bottlenecks. Port authorities around the world must build specialized bunkering facilities to store and supply non-traditional fuels safely. At the same time, shipowners face high capital expenditure costs when deciding whether to retrofit existing vessels or purchase new dual-fuel ships.

To learn more about fuel performance, emission standards, and fleet deployment strategies, consult this detailed maritime decarbonization alternative fuels guide.

Looking Ahead at Ocean Logistics

The transition toward low-emission shipping represents one of the largest engineering and supply chain overhauls in modern history. Over the next decade, global trade will increasingly rely on dual-fuel vessels, digital route optimization, and expanded clean-fuel infrastructure at major ports.

By understanding how cargo moves across maritime supply chains, consumers and businesses can better evaluate the environmental footprint of the products they use every day, encouraging a more sustainable approach to international trade.

text:
Negotiations at the IMO have drawn a blank for the third meeting in a row, as US and Saudi-led efforts to scupper progress were successful, said Transport & Environment (T&E).

With delegates from vulnerable countries highlighting the tragic cost of this year’s climate disasters, action is far too slow, warns T&E.

While negotiators, including the EU, signalled openness to compromise measures such as avoiding a centralised fund and weakening greenhouse gas targets, US and Saudi negotiators largely held their ground.

“The continued failure to find an ambitious common ground not only puts shipping off course to decarbonise, but locks fossil fuel importing states and the shipping industry into continued dependency. During the Hormuz crisis, dependence on oil cost the industry roughly €340 million a day,” according to T&E estimates.

The next major IMO meeting takes place from November 30 to December 3.

Alex Springer, interim shipping director at T&E, said: “After a summer of heatwaves, droughts and record sea temperatures, the failure of states to get close to a credible deal is deeply disappointing. It leaves global shipping increasingly adrift of where it needs to be. Governments should push forward with ambitious regional measures and must not wait for a global agreement before taking action.”

In accordance with UCL Shipping and Oceans Research Group, the IMO’s 22nd Intersessional Working Group on GHG emissions has concluded with significant majority of member states (two thirds of those who took the floor) supporting a centralised system for collecting revenues, operationalized through a GHG price (RU price), and disbursing it for rewards for early adopters and supporting a just and equitable transition.

The group of member states focused on a technical-only solution and abandonment of GHG pricing, remained small and consistently composed of strongly fossil fuel aligned governments.

The Clean Shipping Coalition welcomed broad support by member states for the Net-Zero Framework (NZF), but criticised attempts by a minority of states to undermine it with ‘alternative proposals’ and called for its adoption at December’s Marine Environment Protect Committee.

“Alternative proposals to the Net-Zero Framework are neither necessary nor useful – the IMO has already committed to a strategy, approved a regulatory framework that can deliver it, and scheduled its adoption for later in the year,” said Lukas Leppert, president of the Clean Shipping Coalition. “While not entirely aligned with the levels of ambition in the IMO 2023 GHG Strategy, the NZF is a long-negotiated compromise that brings together a multitude of interests and positions and is supported by a broad majority. We consider the NZF an important step forward and one that can be built on to become more progressive in the future.”

The Intersessional Working Group on Reduction of Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Emissions from Ships (ISWG-GHG 22) met for its 22nd meeting from 1 to 4 September 2026, chaired by Mr. Sveinung Oftedal (Norway), according to the International Maritime Organization on Friday (4 September).

According to a meeting summary by IMO, the meeting had a high level of participation, with nearly 1200 registered participants, in person and online.

During the meeting participants considered the following agenda items:

Consideration of proposals, including documents submitted to MEPC 84 and 85, previous sessions of ISWG-GHG, as well as documents submitted to ISWG-GHG 22, on how to address concerns with the draft amendments to MARPOL Annex VI on the Net-Zero Framework, in line with the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy

Following constructive discussions, the Chair expressed his observation of a genuine willingness within the Group to make concrete further progress at the next ISWG-GHG meeting and work towards presenting text to MEPC 85 that adequately addresses the noted progress made in the consideration of proposals on how to address concerns raised regarding the draft amendments to MARPOL Annex VI on the mid-term measure.

The Group invited interested delegations to continue to consult intersessionally to address remaining concerns with the draft amendments to MARPOL Annex VI, in line with the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, taking into account views expressed at the Group’s session, with a view to submitting concrete proposals reflecting enhanced convergence allowing timely adoption and effective implementation.

Further consideration of the draft guidelines supporting the uniform and effective implementation of IMO’s mid-term measures.

The Group held a preliminary exchange of views on this agenda item, although time became a limiting factor and the Group and agreed to defer the consideration of all documents submitted to this session under this agenda item to ISWG-GHG 23 (23-27 November 2026).

Further consideration of the development of the IMO Life Cycle GHG Assessment (LCA) framework.

Due to time constraints, the Group was not able to consider the agenda item related to the IMO Life Cycle GHG Assessment (LCA) framework. The Group deferred the consideration of those documents to ISWG-GHG 23, in conjunction with the report of the fourth meeting of the GESAMP-LCA Working Group expected to be submitted to MEPC 85.

Next steps

The next meeting of the Intersessional Working Group on Reduction of Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Emissions from Ships (ISWG-GHG 23) is scheduled for 23 to 27 November 2026, ahead of MEPC 85 (30 November to 3 December).

The second extraordinary session of MEPC (adjourned last October) is scheduled to resume on 4 December, subject to discussions at MEPC 85.

Published: 7 September, 2026

UCL Shipping and Oceans Research Group on Friday (4 September) said the IMO’s 22nd Intersessional Working Group on GHG emissions has concluded with significant majority of member states supporting a centralised system for collecting revenues, operationalised through a GHG price (RU price), and disbursing it for rewards for early adopters and supporting a just and equitable transition.

The group of member states focused on a technical-only solution and abandonment of GHG pricing, remained small and consistently composed of strongly fossil fuel aligned governments.

Just as at MEPC 84, the political dynamics observed at MEPC.ES2 did not occur in this meeting.

The discussions were more representative of the ISWG-GHG 19 and MEPC 83 negotiating dynamics, but this does not rule out the potential for the dynamics that occurred at MEPC.ES2 returning in future meetings. That said, there was reassuring evidence from the week that reduces that risk, including in the contrast between strong public (press) positions taken against the IMO’s NZF, and the substance of how delegations negotiated in the meeting.

Dr Tristan Smith, Professor of Energy and Transport at UCL Shipping and Oceans Research Group, said: “Whilst there are many positives to take away – there is clear potential for a return to a strong policy solution and decision making this December, there remains high uncertainty in the extent that both industry’s transition and low-income countries’ transitions will be supported.

“There remains high risk that in the effort to find a creative way forwards, the equilibrium between these two aspects, that enabled the NZF in the first place, is lost to the detriment of the outcome overall.”

In addition to the discussion on centralised system for revenue collection and disbursement, the meeting discussed a number of other items as guided by the chair, discussed in detail with member state positions in the readout. Some of these included:

GFI (Global Fuel Intensity) reduction pathway: GFI is likely to be softened initially (around 2030), but then steeper in the period to 2040.

ZNZ rewards: ZNZ reward still broadly supported and a priority to many member states, but the broad support for a multiplier, despite it being taken off the table at the last meeting, could yet lead this to be incorporated to provide incentivisation.

Compliance approaches:

Most interventions confirmed support for the compliance mechanisms as setup in NZF ‘as is’. The strongest support was for the two least controversial options common to all proposals: reducing GHG intensity and pooling/transfer of SU.

Direct contributions: Japan’s proposal to replace GHG pricing with shipowner-directed contributions was robustly rejected, particularly by the member states that would need to ‘swing’ to support it for this to start to build momentum.

SU (Surplus Units) trading: Majority of member states opposed the inclusion of energy efficiency SU credits and the concept of printing SU’s to manage an SU price shock, citing various reasons, primarily a concern that this would destabilise the SU market and undermine investment predictability.

Netting: China’s proposal to balance of RU and reward payments that could be netted to form a single transaction received broad support. However, the details of the concept will now need to be set out in guidelines and there remain a number of issues regarding this approach, as raised by several delegations.

Classification society Lloyd’s Register (LR) on Thursday (3 September) said it has awarded Approval in Principle (AiP) to CSSC Huangpu Wenchong Shipbuilding Co., Ltd. for a new 12,500 m³ LNG bunkering vessel design.

The AiP was signed at SMM 2026 in Hamburg and confirms that the vessel concept has successfully completed an independent design assessment against LR’s latest classification requirements.

The new 12,500 m³ vessel design incorporates Type C LNG cargo tanks and has been evaluated against a comprehensive range of class notations covering gas operations, automation, environmental performance and cyber resilience.

LR’s assessment was carried out in accordance with its Rules and Regulations for the Classification of Ships and Rules and Regulations for the Construction and Classification of Ships for the Carriage of Liquefied Gas in Bulk.

Constantinos Chaelis, LR’s Global Gas Segment Director, said: “This project demonstrates the continued market confidence in LNG and the importance of building the supporting infrastructure that enables owners to make practical emissions reductions today, while maintaining flexibility for the future. Through early engagement between shipyard and class, we can accelerate the delivery of robust designs that meet both operational and regulatory requirements.”

A Huangpu Wenchong spokesperson, said: “This Approval in Principle from Lloyd’s Register validates the technical approach and provides a strong foundation for future development. We believe vessels of this type will play an increasingly important role in supporting the energy transition by helping ensure LNG is available where shipowners need it most.”

Consideration of proposals, including documents submitted to MEPC 84 and 85, previous sessions of ISWG-GHG, as well as documents submitted to ISWG-GHG 22, on how to address concerns with the draft amendments to MARPOL Annex VI on the Net-Zero Framework, in line with the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy

Following constructive discussions, the Chair expressed his observation of a genuine willingness within the Group to make concrete further progress at the next ISWG-GHG meeting and work towards presenting text to MEPC 85 that adequately addresses the noted progress made in the consideration of proposals on how to address concerns raised regarding the draft amendments to MARPOL Annex VI on the mid-term measure.

The Group invited interested delegations to continue to consult intersessionally to address remaining concerns with the draft amendments to MARPOL Annex VI, in line with the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, taking into account views expressed at the Group’s session, with a view to submitting concrete proposals reflecting enhanced convergence allowing timely adoption and effective implementation.

Further consideration of the draft guidelines supporting the uniform and effective implementation of IMO’s mid-term measures.

The Group held a preliminary exchange of views on this agenda item, although time became a limiting factor and the Group and agreed to defer the consideration of all documents submitted to this session under this agenda item to ISWG-GHG 23 (23-27 November 2026).

Further consideration of the development of the IMO Life Cycle GHG Assessment (LCA) framework.

Due to time constraints, the Group was not able to consider the agenda item related to the IMO Life Cycle GHG Assessment (LCA) framework. The Group deferred the consideration of those documents to ISWG-GHG 23, in conjunction with the report of the fourth meeting of the GESAMP-LCA Working Group expected to be submitted to MEPC 85.

Next steps

The next meeting of the Intersessional Working Group on Reduction of Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Emissions from Ships (ISWG-GHG 23) is scheduled for 23 to 27 November 2026, ahead of MEPC 85 (30 November to 3 December).

The second extraordinary session of MEPC (adjourned last October) is scheduled to resume on 4 December, subject to discussions at MEPC 85.

title: ISWG-GHG 22 discussions signal path back to Net-Zero deal, but political risks remain
description:
According to an analysis by the UCL Shipping and Oceans Research Group, around two-thirds of member states that took the floor supported the revenue-collection approach.
Unlike that meeting, the latest discussions more closely resembled the negotiating patterns observed at ISWG-GHG 19 and MEPC 83.
…said Dr. Tristan Smith, Professor of Energy and Transport at UCL Shipping and Oceans Research Group.
The maritime energy transition will be shaped by the decisions the IMO Member States make over the coming months.
The next major IMO meeting takes place from November 30th to December 3rd.
text:
According to an analysis by the UCL Shipping and Oceans Research Group, around two-thirds of member states that took the floor supported the revenue-collection approach. By contrast, the group advocating a technical-only solution and the abandonment of GHG pricing remained relatively small and was consistently made up of governments closely aligned with fossil-fuel interests.

The political dynamics also differed markedly from those seen at MEPC.ES2. Unlike that meeting, the latest discussions more closely resembled the negotiating patterns observed at ISWG-GHG 19 and MEPC 83. That said, there was reassuring evidence from the week that reduces that risk, including in the contrast between strong public positions taken against the IMO’s NZF, and the substance of how delegations negotiated in the meeting.

The meeting also explored a number of innovative approaches that could, in theory, make the GHG-pricing and fund elements more acceptable to the NZF’s detractors. Refining these proposals is likely to be a central focus of work ahead of ISWG-GHG 23 and MEPC 85.

How the pricing and funding mechanisms are ultimately designed could determine the balance of support for two critical elements of the transition: incentives for zero- or near-zero-emission (ZNZ) fuels and technologies, particularly to encourage early adoption of long-term solutions, and financial support for low-income countries seeking to deliver a Just and Equitable Transition (JET), with the discussions also highlighting the political trade-off between these two priorities.

Significant changes to the size of the fund or the scope of how its revenues can be used could shift the balance of support among Member States, potentially strengthening backing for one objective at the expense of the other.

Whilst there are many positives to take away – there is clear potential for a return to a strong policy solution and decision making this December, there remains high uncertainty in the extent that both industry’s transition and low-income countries’ transitions will be supported. There remains high risk that in the effort to find a creative way forwards, the equilibrium between these two aspects, that enabled the NZF in the first place, is lost to the detriment of the outcome overall.

…said Dr. Tristan Smith, Professor of Energy and Transport at UCL Shipping and Oceans Research Group.

In addition to the discussion on centralised system for revenue collection and disbursement, the meeting discussed a number of other items as guided by the chair, discussed in detail with member state positions in the readout.

Dr. Annika Frosch, Research Fellow at UCL Shipping and Oceans Research Group said: “Despite the intense debate over its design, a clear majority of delegations still regard a Fund, Facility, or similar financial structure as essential to implementing the 2023 IMO Strategy. Their message is clear: without predictable financing, there can be no credible Just and Equitable Transition.”

Taken together, the evidence suggests that the IMO’s Net-Zero Framework (NZF), broadly as currently designed, remains the most obvious and widely supported path forward.

The political challenge, however, lies in formally reaching that conclusion. The negotiations may therefore focus less on fundamentally changing the framework than on constructing a package that appears new while ultimately delivering broadly similar outcomes.

A reduction in JET support could prove politically consequential. A number of low-income countries that currently favour clear mitigation requirements and binding obligations could reconsider their positions, potentially backing weaker or more ambiguous provisions instead.

Such an outcome could increase uncertainty for investors and, in turn, raise the risks and costs associated with the shipping sector’s transition.

The maritime energy transition will be shaped by the decisions the IMO Member States make over the coming months. As the professional body representing the technical voice of maritime professionals worldwide, the IMarEST is proud to support Member States in navigating these complex choices […]

…noted Alasdair Wishart, Institute of Marine Engineering, Science and Technology (IMarEST) Technical and Policy Director.

T&E: IMO fails to break deadlock

Transport & Environment (T&E) commented that the IMO negotiations have ended in ‘deadlock’ for the third consecutive meeting, with US- and Saudi-led opposition once again blocking progress. As delegates from climate-vulnerable countries pointed to the devastating toll of this year’s climate disasters, T&E warned that action to decarbonise shipping is moving far too slowly.

While pragmatic negotiators, including the EU, signalled openness to compromise measures such as avoiding a centralised fund and weakening greenhouse gas targets, US and Saudi negotiators largely held their ground.

T&E urged negotiators not to cave to the Trump administration’s crusade to sacrifice ambitious targets in favor of fossil gas and crop biofuels – a lose-lose deal for the climate and for future-proofing the industry.

After a summer of heatwaves, droughts and record sea temperatures, the failure of states to get close to a credible deal is deeply disappointing. It leaves global shipping increasingly adrift of where it needs to be. Governments should push forward with ambitious regional measures and must not wait for a global agreement before taking action.

…said Alex Springer, interim shipping director at T&E.

The next major IMO meeting takes place from November 30th to December 3rd. There, governments must adopt a global deal capable of decarbonising shipping by 2050, rather than giving up on the climate or delaying action again. T&E urged delegations to intensify diplomatic efforts to overcome the obstruction of the US and its allies.

title: IMO weighs softer 2030 emissions target to revive Net Zero Framework - gasworld
description:
A potential compromise to weaken the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) emissions requirements around 2030 could reduce early demand for hydrogen-derived fuels, as governments seek to revive the regulator’s stalled Net Zero Framework (NZF).
IMO member states discussed adjusting the framework’s greenhouse gas fuel intensity (GFI) trajectory during negotiations in London from 1 to 4 September, with an emerging landing zone understood to involve less stringent requirements around 2030.
By 2030, the framework set a base GFI reduction target of 8% and a more stringent “direct compliance” target of 21%.
It was upended in 2025 after a coalition of member states voted against the carbon pricing elements of the framework.
Now nations are mulling a less stringent 2030 target before ramping up ambition toward 2040.
text:
A potential compromise to weaken the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) emissions requirements around 2030 could reduce early demand for hydrogen-derived fuels, as governments seek to revive the regulator’s stalled Net Zero Framework (NZF).

IMO member states discussed adjusting the framework’s greenhouse gas fuel intensity (GFI) trajectory during negotiations in London from 1 to 4 September, with an emerging landing zone understood to involve less stringent requirements around 2030.

Under the original IMO proposal, ships would have been required to progressively reduce the lifecycle greenhouse gas intensity (GFI) of the energy they use, compared with a reference value of 93.3gCO2e/MJ.

By 2030, the framework set a base GFI reduction target of 8% and a more stringent “direct compliance” target of 21%. Ships failing to meet the targets would face compliance costs, while those outperforming the stricter threshold could generate surplus compliance units.

It was upended in 2025 after a coalition of member states voted against the carbon pricing elements of the framework. Now nations are mulling a less stringent 2030 target before ramping up ambition toward 2040.

Such a compromise could make the framework more politically acceptable, but would also reduce the pressure on shipowners to decarbonise during the early years of the regulation.

That could have implications for proposed green hydrogen projects targeting the maritime sector, particularly producers of green ammonia and e-methanol seeking long-term offtake agreements with shipowners.

Many such projects are targeting start-up around the end of this decade or the early 2030s, meaning a weaker initial GFI trajectory could coincide with the period in which developers need new sources of demand to underpin investment decisions.

However, a softer trajectory could ultimately prove more valuable for developers if it allows IMO members to agree to the adoption of the NZF after it was postponed last year.

Financial rewards for ships using zero- or near-zero-emission fuels also appear likely to remain part of the framework, potentially offsetting some of the impact of weaker near-term GFI requirements on hydrogen-derived fuels.

The precise shape of any revised trajectory has yet to be agreed. Governments have been asked to develop compromise proposals ahead of the next round of IMO negotiations in November, immediately before the Marine Environment Protection Committee meets to consider the framework.

text:
LONDRA – Prosegue all’IMO il confronto sulle misure per ridurre le emissioni di gas serra del trasporto marittimo internazionale. Dal 1° al 4 Settembre si è riunito il 22° Intersessional Working Group on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships (ISWG-GHG 22), con una partecipazione particolarmente ampia: quasi 1.200 delegati, presenti fisicamente e collegati da remoto. Al centro dei lavori sono rimaste le modifiche alla MARPOL Annex VI necessarie per introdurre il cosiddetto Net-Zero Framework, in attuazione della strategia IMO 2023 sulla riduzione delle emissioni di gas serra delle navi.

Il confronto ha evidenziato alcuni progressi nella ricerca di un punto di convergenza sulle misure di medio periodo, ma non ha ancora consentito di chiudere le questioni più controverse. Il presidente del gruppo, il norvegese Sveinung Oftedal, ha sottolineato la disponibilità delle delegazioni a proseguire il lavoro e a compiere ulteriori passi avanti in vista della prossima sessione. Le delegazioni interessate sono state quindi invitate a proseguire le consultazioni tra una riunione e l’altra, elaborando proposte concrete che possano contribuire a superare le divergenze ancora esistenti e consentire un’adozione tempestiva delle nuove regole.

Linee guida e valutazione del ciclo di vita

Il programma dell’ISWG-GHG 22 prevedeva anche l’esame delle linee guida per l’applicazione uniforme ed efficace delle misure di medio periodo dell’IMO. Su questo punto, tuttavia, il tempo a disposizione non è stato sufficiente per un esame approfondito della documentazione. La discussione è stata pertanto rinviata alla prossima sessione del gruppo di lavoro, in programma a novembre.

Lo stesso è accaduto per il quadro IMO sulla Life Cycle GHG Assessment (LCA), cioè il sistema destinato a valutare le emissioni di gas serra lungo l’intero ciclo di vita dei combustibili e delle soluzioni energetiche utilizzate nel settore marittimo. Anche i documenti relativi a questo dossier saranno esaminati durante l’ISWG-GHG 23, insieme al rapporto del quarto meeting del gruppo di lavoro GESAMP-LCA.

Il sostegno ai Paesi in via di sviluppo

Durante la riunione è stato inoltre fatto il punto sul Voluntary Multi-Donor Trust Fund, il fondo istituito dall’IMO per favorire la partecipazione dei Paesi in via di sviluppo, in particolare dei piccoli Stati insulari (SIDS) e dei Paesi meno sviluppati (LDC), ai lavori sul clima e sulla decarbonizzazione del trasporto marittimo. Dal 2023 il fondo ha finanziato la partecipazione di 225 delegati provenienti da 58 Paesi, tra riunioni MEPC, ISWG-GHG e incontri del comitato direttivo. Alla sessione appena conclusa ha consentito la partecipazione di rappresentanti di 32 Paesi.

Il fondo rischia però di chiudere il 2026 con un deficit di circa 220 mila sterline, legato soprattutto all’aumento dei costi di viaggio. L’IMO ha quindi rivolto un nuovo appello agli Stati membri e alle organizzazioni internazionali affinché contribuiscano al finanziamento dello strumento e ne garantiscano la continuità.

Appuntamento a Novembre

Il confronto sulla decarbonizzazione dello shipping entrerà ora nella fase successiva. La 23ª sessione dell’ISWG-GHG è fissata dal 23 al 27 Novembre 2026, immediatamente prima della 85ª sessione del Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 85), prevista dal 30 Novembre al 3 Dicembre. Proprio in vista di questi appuntamenti dovranno essere affrontate le questioni ancora aperte sul Net-Zero Framework, sulle linee guida applicative e sul sistema di valutazione del ciclo di vita dei combustibili.

Il secondo MEPC straordinario, la cui sessione era stata aggiornata lo scorso Ottobre, dovrebbe infine riprendere i lavori il 4 Dicembre, subordinatamente agli sviluppi della riunione MEPC 85.

name: IMO & Shipping
title: Cyprus shipping caught between investment decisions and unfinished IMO rules
description:
Cyprus shipping faces another period of uncertainty after four days of negotiations at the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) ended without an agreed new text for the global rules intended to steer international shipping towards net zero.
The September meeting forms part of a much longer attempt to turn the IMO’s climate ambitions into binding global shipping rules.
Under the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, international shipping is expected to reach net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by or around 2050.
It also emphasised the importance of a solution capable of maintaining a level playing field for international shipping while meeting environmental objectives.
For Cyprus-based shipowners and managers, the concern is that major investment decisions cannot simply be postponed until every part of the IMO framework has been settled.
text:
Cyprus shipping faces another period of uncertainty after four days of negotiations at the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) ended without an agreed new text for the global rules intended to steer international shipping towards net zero.

The 22nd session of the IMO working group, held in London from September 1 to 4, brought together nearly 1,200 participants, both in person and online, as governments attempted to narrow remaining differences over the organisation’s Net-Zero Framework.

The meeting did not abandon the framework. However, it also failed to resolve the concerns that have prevented its final adoption, leaving some of the most commercially important details for another negotiating round in November.

According to the IMO, discussions focused on proposals submitted to MEPC 84 and 85, previous working-group sessions and ISWG-GHG 22 itself, all aimed at addressing concerns surrounding the proposed amendments to MARPOL Annex VI.

Following the talks, working-group chairman Sveinung Oftedal observed what the IMO described as a “genuine willingness” among participants to make further progress and work towards presenting a text to MEPC 85 capable of reflecting greater convergence.

Delegations were consequently invited to continue consultations between meetings and submit concrete proposals addressing the remaining concerns, with the IMO seeking what it described as “timely adoption and effective implementation”.

The September meeting forms part of a much longer attempt to turn the IMO’s climate ambitions into binding global shipping rules.

Under the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, international shipping is expected to reach net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by or around 2050.

The strategy also calls for total annual greenhouse gas emissions from international shipping to fall by at least 20 per cent by 2030, while striving for 30 per cent, compared with 2008 levels.

By 2040, the reduction should reach at least 70 per cent, while striving for 80 per cent.

At the same time, zero or near-zero greenhouse gas emission technologies, fuels and energy sources should represent at least 5 per cent of shipping’s energy use by 2030, with the IMO striving for 10 per cent.

Turning those ambitions into rules has proved considerably more difficult.

The IMO Net-Zero Framework was approved by MEPC 83 in April 2025 as a proposed new Chapter 5 of MARPOL Annex VI.

It contains two closely connected elements.

The first is a global marine fuel standard requiring ships progressively to reduce the greenhouse gas intensity of the energy they use.

The second is a global GHG emissions pricing mechanism, intended to create a financial cost for ships that fail to meet the required levels while rewarding cleaner alternatives.

The rules are intended to apply to oceangoing ships above 5,000 gross tonnage, a group responsible for more than 85 per cent of global shipping emissions, according to the IMO.

However, the framework has yet to complete the process required for it to become legally binding.

It had been scheduled for adoption during the second extraordinary session of the Marine Environment Protection Committee in October 2025.

Instead, the IMO adjourned that session for a year, allowing member states more time to work towards consensus.

The process continued at MEPC 84 earlier this year, when member states agreed to hold two additional intersessional meetings, the first in September and the second in November, in an attempt to address outstanding concerns before MEPC 85.

The September round has now ended without that work being completed.

Moreover, the disagreement is not limited to the broad political architecture of the framework.

Detailed rules still have to explain how the system will work in practice.

Previous IMO working-group discussions have covered guidelines for fuel certification, zero and near-zero emission fuels and their rewards, operation of the IMO Net-Zero Fund, calculation of ships’ GHG Fuel Intensity, compliance options and the planned IMO GFI Registry.

Those details matter directly to shipowners because they will determine not simply whether a vessel complies, but also how particular fuels and technologies are treated financially under the system.

At ISWG-GHG 22, however, the group managed only a preliminary exchange of views on the guidelines needed for uniform and effective implementation.

With time running out, all documents submitted under the item were deferred to ISWG-GHG 23, scheduled for November 23 to 27.

Another important piece of the regulatory puzzle was also postponed.

The group was unable to consider documents concerning the IMO’s Life Cycle GHG Assessment framework, again because of time constraints.

These will now be considered in November alongside the expected report from the fourth meeting of the GESAMP-LCA Working Group.

The life-cycle rules are particularly significant for investment decisions because the IMO intends emissions to be considered on a well-to-wake basis.

That means the greenhouse gas impact of a fuel is not limited to what comes out of a ship’s exhaust.

Emissions associated with producing and supplying the fuel are also taken into account, potentially changing the relative attractiveness of fuels that may appear cleaner when only their use on board is considered.

For shipowners deciding between conventional fuels, biofuels, LNG, methanol, ammonia and other emerging alternatives, the final methodology can therefore have significant commercial consequences.

The same applies to the financial mechanism contained in the framework.

Under the draft MARPOL amendments, initial remedial unit prices for the 2028-2030 reporting periods were set at $100 per tonne of CO₂ equivalent for Tier 1 and $380 per tonne for Tier 2, calculated on a well-to-wake basis.

Ships performing above the required levels may generate surplus units, while ships failing to meet their targets would have to address their compliance deficits through available surplus units or remedial units linked to payments into the Net-Zero Fund.

For Cyprus, the uncertainty surrounding those details is particularly relevant.

According to the Shipping Deputy Ministry, Cyprus has the third-largest fleet in Europe and the 11th largest globally, while companies operating from the island manage more than 20 per cent of the world’s third-party managed fleet.

Limassol alone hosts more than 200 shipping and shipping-related companies, ranging from shipowners and shipmanagers to insurers, financiers, brokers and maritime technology providers.

The Cyprus Shipping Chamber (CSC) has consequently been among those calling for a global solution capable of giving international shipping a common regulatory framework.

Following MEPC 84 in May, the Chamber welcomed the decision to continue intensive negotiations, while stressing that the eventual system needs to be practical, effective and globally applicable.

It also emphasised the importance of a solution capable of maintaining a level playing field for international shipping while meeting environmental objectives.

Chamber director general Alexandros Josephides attended MEPC 84 as part of the Shipping Deputy Ministry delegation, with the Chamber saying it remained committed to supporting sustainable but realistic solutions for the sector.

For Cyprus-based shipowners and managers, the concern is that major investment decisions cannot simply be postponed until every part of the IMO framework has been settled.

A vessel ordered today for delivery towards the end of the decade could remain in service well beyond 2050.

Decisions over engines, fuel capability, retrofitting possibilities and other technologies must therefore be made while the financial treatment of those choices under the future global system is still being finalised.

A fuel or propulsion option that appears commercially attractive today could become more expensive once its full life-cycle emissions are calculated.

Conversely, technologies carrying a higher initial cost could become more attractive if the eventual rules give them access to rewards or lower compliance costs.

There is also a broader issue for shipping companies attempting to plan fleets over several decades.

Once the framework is adopted, MARPOL procedures mean the regulations would be expected to enter into force 16 months later, leaving a relatively short period between regulatory certainty and practical application.

The next opportunity to close the remaining gaps will come at ISWG-GHG 23 from November 23 to 27.

That meeting will be followed almost immediately by MEPC 85 from November 30 to December 3, when member states will again consider the future of the framework.

The second extraordinary session of MEPC, originally adjourned in October 2025, is then scheduled to resume on December 4, subject to the discussions and decisions taken at MEPC 85.

Until then, the IMO Net-Zero Framework remains very much alive.

text:
A relatively ambitious deal to reduce the shipping industry's 3% of global emissions now looks more likely after four days of closed-door talks in London, observers say.

The International Maritime Organization (IMO), which oversees the negotiations, said there had been "constructive discussions" and "genuine willingness within the group to make concrete further progress".

Em Fenton, senior director at the NGO Opportunity Green who attended the talks last week, said they "demonstrated a strong spirit of solidarity in the face of blatant attempts to undermine the credibility, ambition and equity of a hard-fought multilateral agreement".

After several years of debate, governments provisionally agreed in April 2025 on a "Net-Zero Framework" (NZF) - a series of emissions reduction targets for shipowners aimed at incentivising them to use cleaner fuels, backed up with financial rewards for meeting the targets and fees for missing them.

But in October 2025, after a high-profile intervention by US President Donald Trump and threats of US sanctions and visa restrictions, the US convinced a majority of voting nations to postpone the adoption of the NZF for a year.

UCL analysis found that, of those who expressed a view at last week's talks, 38 were in favour of an NZF-style solution while only 17 were against. Those opposed are "consistently composed of strongly fossil fuel-aligned governments".

An observer of the talks, who did not want to be named, said the countries opposed include the US, Russia, India, Thailand, Argentina, Ecuador and Uruguay, as well as eight oil-rich Gulf nations and shipowner-reliant Liberia and Panama. Governments that support an NZF-style deal include China, Brazil, Mexico, Türkiye, Canada, Australia, Chile, nine African nations, most European countries and small islands.

A new framework to tackle shipping emissions could be adopted if two-thirds of countries that are present and signed up to a regulation called Marpol Annex VI - endorsed by just over 100 states - vote in favour of it, as they did in April 2025.

UCL's analysis said it was "reassuring" that governments which had taken strong positions in the media against the NZF were being more compromising in the negotiations.

Tweaks are probable

While there is majority support for the NZF, UCL said adopting it would be difficult politically. "The process from here could therefore be as much about producing what appears to be a new package, but one that broadly ends up with similar outcomes in relation to objectives," UCL argued.

But tweaking the NZF, which resulted from years of negotiations, comes with risks, it warned. For example, changes could reduce the new system's planned support for low-income countries, turning them against it. Fenton said compromising should not mean "abandoning the principle of justice in the maritime transition".

UCL said the speed at which shipowners must reduce their ships' emissions or face fees is likely to be reduced in the short-term but raised in the long-term to meet a goal of net zero emissions by mid-century.

This was a compromise put forward by NZF-supporter Brazil. However, an analysis by the the Institute of Marine Engineering, Science and Technology (IMarEST) has found that this change would lead to more overall emissions than the original NZF trajectory.

UCL has warned it could incentivise liquefied natural gas as a shipping fuel over greener options, which include hydrogen-based methanol and ammonia.

Analysis by UCL and the Rocky Mountain Institute suggests that, while a slower start to the NZF would reduce transport costs in the short term, it would increase them later due to the costs involved in switching the industry over from more polluting fuel to cleaner fuel.

NZF won't meet emissions goals

IMarEst's analysis finds that even in its current form - the most ambitious deal on the table - the NZF will not be sufficient for shipping to meet its emissions reduction goals.

It says that only a Pacific proposal to place a levy on ships' total emissions - rather than just those above a certain level - would meet the industry's targets to reduce emissions 20% between 2008 and 2030, 70% by 2040 and then reach net zero "by or around, i.e. close to 2050". This is highly unlikely to be adopted.

Additional talks will be held from November 23-27 and from November 30-December 3 before a potentially final round of official negotiations begins on December 4.
